title: Mike Africa Jr On Philly Move Bombing & The Move 9
summary: Our Hidden History · 2024-08-16 · Officer Abdon with Mike Africa Jr.
body:
Our Hidden History · 2024-08-16 · Officer Abdon, with Mike Africa Jr.

Opens [Eccl 7](/bible/ecclesiastes/7)
## Introduction *[[0:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=10s)]* **Officer Abdon:** Shalom, Israel. Most High Christ bless. Officer Abdon here. We're on the set for Our Hidden History in IUIC Philadelphia. Today we have a special, special guest. A lot of us know or have heard of the bombing that took place in Philadelphia in 1985, the MOVE movement. But a lot of us don't know any history prior to it, what led to it, or anything that happened to those members after. Today we have with us a good brother that has relations to those in the movement, and he himself is a part of the MOVE movement. We have today Mike Africa Jr. How you doing, sir? **Mike Africa Jr.:** I'm feeling great. How you doing today? **Officer Abdon:** I'm doing great, man. All praise the Most High. It's good to see another Philly resident, born and raised in Philly. **Mike Africa Jr.:** Correct. Born and raised West Philly. **Officer Abdon:** West Philly. All praise the Most High. So brother Mike, what is your relation to the MOVE movement? *[[1:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=71s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** The MOVE Organization is my family. Like it or not, love it or not, crazy or not, the organization is my family. A lot of people joined the organization. You know, they had troubled pasts, they had issues with their families or whatever, and they needed to get away from society, whatever was going on with them. That wasn't me. I was born into it. The founder of the organization, John Africa, is my uncle, my great uncle, my grandmother's brother. He started the organization. My grandmother was a member of the organization. My great aunt Louise, who owned the house on Osage Avenue, she was a member. Her son was a member. My grandmother had five children; they were all members. My father was a member. So half of the organization was my blood family. **Officer Abdon:** Wow. **Mike Africa Jr.:** So that's how I am connected to it. *[[2:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=125s)]* **Officer Abdon:** A lot of times we hear from the past revolutionists, it's always about, okay, I joined because of this. But you yourself was actually in the family of the movement. **Mike Africa Jr.:** That's right. But here's the thing about that. You know how it is: your mother takes you to church, to the mosque or to the synagogue, whatever place of worship that your family is involved in. And unless you yourself decide that you want to be that, you're not that. You can be taken to church, but that doesn't make you a Christian. **Officer Abdon:** Very true. **Mike Africa Jr.:** You can be taken to the mosque or the mass, but that does not make you a Muslim. **Officer Abdon:** So what made you be a part of the MOVE? **Mike Africa Jr.:** Right. So I decided that I wanted to be a part of it. Once I knew that my parents were in prison, and once I could understand that there is a system that is targeting us, that is hurting us, that is causing us problems, I just wanted to do something about it. And that was made easy for me, to tap into something that was already doing something about it, in MOVE. So I decided I wanted to be a part of it, and then that just took its natural progression. ## Readings and Scriptures *[[3:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=210s)]* **Officer Abdon:** So what was the MOVE movement actually about? Because a lot of us, even in Philadelphia, we hear the MOVE movement, it relates to the bombing, but a lot of us don't know what the MOVE movement was. **Mike Africa Jr.:** Right. The organization's mission was protect life: people, animals and the environment. And having that mission, if you see a brother being accosted by police and your mission is to protect life, you going to get involved. You got something to say. If you see that brother get sent to jail for an obscene amount of time, some unjust jail sentence, you got something to say about that. But it's not just about people, it's also about animals. If you see a black man, a black woman, Africans, being brought to this country in chains, and you have a problem with that, you protest about that. We want freedom, we want equality. All right, well then the same system that put the Africans in chains, it's the same system that put the lion in the crate and shipped them over here and put them in chains in the zoo. And so if that system is allowed to do that to animals... At one time they looked at us as animals, and they still do. So the equality that we talking about, how can we ever achieve it if we allow prejudice to exist? And that same thing is carried over to women, it's carried over to children, it's carried over to black people, Asian people. And prejudice is so inherent in this American system, in the world system, and if we're going to ever have freedom and equality, got to get rid of it. *[[5:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=306s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** So MOVE said, okay, we're going to do something about it. So John Africa started writing about it and talking about where it comes from, and these politicians and how they uphold and support it. And as you know, this Frank Rizzo person, **Officer Abdon:** Yes. **Mike Africa Jr.:** this racist mayor, or police commissioner turned mayor, who didn't like anything that had anything to do with black men or progression for black anything. So MOVE and Frank Rizzo clashed. And he had law enforcement on his side, and MOVE had ourselves most of the time, and some members from the community, but for the most part it was like MOVE against the world. That's how MOVE felt about it anyway. **Officer Abdon:** And that's how almost every black revolutionary group or movement is. It's always them against the world, where they put on hate group lists or everything like that. It's always them against the world. Propaganda. **Mike Africa Jr.:** You know, the most frustrating thing about that is the people that are fighting for change get criticized for that fight. **Officer Abdon:** Yeah. **Mike Africa Jr.:** People are so ignorant sometimes. Like, I have so many family members that hate MOVE, because MOVE took a stand, and blame MOVE for what happened to MOVE because of the stand they took. But they don't feel the same way about the system that made MOVE feel compelled to resist. **Officer Abdon:** Right. **Mike Africa Jr.:** You know, they are the same people that every Black History Month, they want to clap, clap, clap it up. They want to: Martin Luther King was this, that. And I promise you Martin Luther King agrees more with me than he does with them. But they are so shallow. And they want to act like we caused a problem, because we shouldn't have been making noise, MOVE shouldn't have been making noise. But at the same time, Black History Month come around, Martin Luther King's birthday, if Malcolm X day is around, they all front and center acting like they with it. **Officer Abdon:** A lot of people are comfortable with the way society runs, so they don't ever feel a need to go against the grain to make a change. Even if they see things going wrong with their own family members, with the system that has their own family in the prisons, they will never say anything. *[[7:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=447s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** Man, we got two idiotic presidential candidates right now. **Officer Abdon:** Yes we do. Yes we do. **Mike Africa Jr.:** And the black people is dancing for them. Oh man, we about to have a first woman of color. Oh man, can you dig it? It is so stupid. And people don't even realize or investigate what people are about before they start throwing their support their way. You could have a person that don't have the presidential accolades, don't have any of the credentials to say what they've accomplished, but they have a body of work throughout the years in the community, doing all of this amazing work, helping people, supporting people that really need it, and they're making a major impact. But because they're not put in front of the bright lights and on the presidential ticket, they'll never get support. Anybody that will have their artists perform for a politician, but won't have those same artists perform for support for this lady who just got shot in the face by the police, **Officer Abdon:** Yes, sir. **Mike Africa Jr.:** this a problem. It's a problem not only for the black community, and the message that it sends; it's also a problem for the families that really can't get the kind of support that they need, in these times of trauma, in these times of harm. And the system really, they do a really good job of keeping black people stupid. *[[9:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=552s)]* **Officer Abdon:** That's very true. And even when you mentioned about Rizzo, I know a lot of people relate him to J. Edgar Hoover, with his belief as far as the worst thing that can happen to America is Negro unity. So any movement that happened, the problem that they had wasn't with the movement's ideals; it was that Negroes were coming together and thinking together against the system. And I like what in COINTELPRO they was talking about as far as the leaders. Because you brought up the two presidential leaders, how our people like to just jump to whoever is the face for black people. But in their writings they talk about how if there's a leader set up, the only leader that's going to be set up for black people is going to be set up by them. So a lot of us just jump to it, but not knowing that they're the ones that setting it up. **Mike Africa Jr.:** And you could show that game plan to people in the black community, and oftentimes those words will fall on deaf ears. They don't care. **Officer Abdon:** Very true. **Mike Africa Jr.:** The system has done a really good job of keeping people stupid. Now there's a few of us, there's a lot of us actually, but it's not enough of us, you know what I'm saying? We really got to start doing a better job ourselves of educating our community, and pushing them to get beyond this shucking and jiving nonsense that they call freedom. **Officer Abdon:** Right. And that's why it's very important, the tour that you're doing, the books, the docu-series, even the things that we're doing right now, to have that conversation. Because if you leave it to our oppressors, educating our children, that's a foolish thing. The most foolish thing you can do is allow your enemies to educate your children. That's the most foolish thing you can do. *[[11:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=668s)]* **Officer Abdon:** So with the MOVE movement, brother Mike, what was the disconnect? Because I've heard the reports. They said, oh, the community was complaining about MOVE, or the police was complaining about MOVE. What was the disconnect between MOVE and the community? **Mike Africa Jr.:** The disconnect between MOVE and the community was that MOVE was very... Well, let me take you back. In the beginning there was no disconnect. MOVE was cool in the community. I mean, they lived the way they lived. They had some ideas that were a little weird. Dreadlocks: dreadlocks were not popular in 1970-something. Oh, they popular now. You watch the Olympics, you see dreadlocks in every category; somebody got something that looked like dreadlocks. But in 1970-something, it wasn't like that. It wasn't even like that in 1980-something. First time I saw a popularized version of locks was Bob Marley, and he wasn't even famous yet. That was in the early 80s. I mean, he was famous in certain places, but he wasn't the global icon that he is today. Whoopi Goldberg, *Jumping Jack Flash*, 1984, 85 maybe, somewhere around there. And then in 1988 Tracy Chapman was on the Grammys and she had these tiny little locks. But in the 70s with MOVE, nah. They was like, where these people look like they come from? Mars? *[[12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=750s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** And the community was like, yo, these guys is extra strong. Women doing 100 push-ups. My mom was eight months pregnant, doing 100. My mom put her foot up on the stool so her belly don't touch the ground, and she do 100 push-ups straight. The police out there challenge them; they couldn't beat them. **Officer Abdon:** Wow. **Mike Africa Jr.:** So they're like, what is up with these people? And they would say, well, how do y'all get so strong like this? And they say, well, because we eat according to nature. We eat raw food. Well, raw food is a popular thing for people to talk about eating now, but in 1970-something, I can assure you it was not. **Officer Abdon:** You eating a raw sweet potato, it still ain't. If I tell people I eat raw sweet potatoes, or eat onions like apples, they'd be like, yo man, ain't nobody trying to do that. Let me get the stove real quick, join it up with some cinnamon. **Mike Africa Jr.:** It ain't popular. And back then it was even less so. So MOVE was looked at as kind of strange. John Africa was kind of eccentric. Like, what is this guy? He got these dogs, he walking dogs for money, and he watching people's cars for free. So people was like, what is this? But when you hear him talk about the system... John Africa say, man, I ain't working no job. I work for the people. They need their car washed, I'll wash their car for them, and if they want to give me something, I'll take that. Great, thank you. And then before you know it, they got a car wash, and they got cars wrapped around the block waiting to get their car washed by a MOVE car wash, making $500 a day. *[[14:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=855s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** Tax man come around, talking about, we need some of that money. You owe us some of that money. We estimate that y'all make $500, $700 a day, and Uncle Sam ain't seen none of that money. John Africa said, did Uncle Sam wash a hubcap? Did Uncle Sam wash one of these windows? Did Uncle Sam put any cleanser in his buckets and carry them across the street? If the answer is no, then Uncle Sam ain't getting none of this money. Remember Michael Vick? You remember Michael Vick? **Officer Abdon:** Yeah, I remember Michael Vick. **Mike Africa Jr.:** Got in trouble for fighting dogs, remember that? He went to jail for it. Actually, he didn't go to jail for fighting the dogs. He went to jail because he made money off of fighting the dogs and he didn't give Uncle Sam none of that money. They didn't care nothing about the dogs. They care about you scamming the system. So that's what it was. Then John Africa said, man, look, take the meter off of the water supply line and just put a regular pipe. We ain't paying for water. **Officer Abdon:** Wow. That's funny. They tried to do the same thing with Christ in the scriptures. The people came and say, hey, does your master pay taxes? So Peter came, like, yo, did he pay taxes? Say, yeah, we pay taxes. But let me ask you something, Peter: do people receive tribute from their children, or from strangers? He said, from strangers. So if we paying taxes, are we free? So he's telling, look, we going to pay taxes, not to offend, but guess what, I'm showing you that we're in slavery still. That's what a lot of people don't understand about the movement. Christ had the biggest, quote unquote, black movement of all the years, but he understood that we weren't free. *[[15:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=948s)]* **Officer Abdon:** I know with Black Panthers and every black liberation movement, they had the understanding that we may not get out of this alive, or we may be imprisoned. Was that the same mindset that you guys had with John Africa when they started the MOVE? **Mike Africa Jr.:** John Africa said, don't let them take you alive. He was like, man, you'd rather be dead than to be caught up in the system, and caught up in their enslavement. He was very extreme like that. I would say John Africa fully understood. Some of the organization members were younger, and they really didn't understand what it was. A lot of people were John Africa's nieces and nephews, so they were just helping Uncle out. They were just being a part of it because they were watching cars, making a couple dollars. Some people didn't understand it. But the core members that were part of the movement of it, they knew. Some of them were ex-Panthers, some of them were ex-military, some of them spent time in Vietnam during the Vietnam War. So they were very aware that there's a system that has a thing going on, and because we protesting against it, we could get killed, we could go to prison. *[[17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1036s)]* **Officer Abdon:** Is that where the militant aspect came from, those that came from the Black Panthers and from the war? **Mike Africa Jr.:** No. The militant aspect of it came from people just being personally tired of it. You know what I'm saying? I can't even walk down the street without getting harassed and accosted by the police. My brother is in a retirement home, and the workers just stealing his money. But because he black, ain't nobody doing nothing about it. Now my brother is hungry. He got one leg, he in the wheelchair, and he can't even do for himself, and there's no system within that system there to help care for him. So I'm going to go complain about it. All right. So the people I complain to, it falls on deaf ears, because they don't care. He's just a black … from Philly, that don't nobody care about. So forget him. So, okay, let's take it to the next level. We can't get justice nowhere. Well, then if we can't get justice anywhere, then what is the tax money that you trying to take from me paying for? So I'm giving you no tax money. You want to get the tax money, you go get it from the people that you support. And if you ain't trying to help us with what we trying to do, then we ain't trying to help you with what you trying to do. So it's an escalation. People are tired of it. *[[18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1119s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** You know how many people was just Netflixing, chilling, when Sonya Massey got killed? And I'm just, man, we snuggled up next to my little baby, we about to chill, we about to watch, get some popcorn, put some butter on, extra salt, because you know we like salt. And we going to just chill. And then news reports of this killing come up, and we got to turn the TV off. We got to turn this TV off, because I can't just Netflix and chill knowing that this white racist man just shot this lady in the face, and then try to cover it up by saying it was self-inflicted, and then trying to call her crazy …. And in front of all of these other police officers. How you going to tell me that there's a few bad apples in the police department? How does that ever make sense? How do people let that slide? How do people get away with that? It's probably the exact opposite. If there's just a few bad apples, then what's wrong with all of these cops that are standing around listening to this man after he shot her in the face, and do nothing? I bet you they wouldn't have did that if somebody shot a police officer in the face. **Officer Abdon:** That's true. **Mike Africa Jr.:** I bet you they wouldn't have did that if their mother was shot in the face. You see what I'm saying? So it's like people just get tired of it. *[[19:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1199s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** I do believe that there is a natural element within people, that God sends them to fight and to help show people the way. I do believe that. I also believe that that is an evolutionary element that came about because people are dictators, and somebody got to fight against it. With the way people are and the way the system is, somebody has to fight against it, because it's wrong. But I don't believe that there are any really just natural born rebels. I believe that people are compelled to become that way because of the issues that we're dealing with all the time. **Officer Abdon:** That's very true. I agree with that. **Mike Africa Jr.:** You know what I'm saying? **Officer Abdon:** I definitely agree with that. **Mike Africa Jr.:** Like Huey wasn't no rebel. Huey, he's a scholar, man. Let me go to education, you know, get some schooling real quick. You know what I'm saying? Can we get a stop light on the corner, though, because people get hit by cars? Can we get some food for these kids? Because back in the day, when you go home for lunch, some kids ain't got no home to go home to for lunch like that. So they just staying at the school, they far away, they can't go home to get something. So, yo, can we get some food for these kids so they can stay while you giving them this reading, writing and arithmetic to do? No, we ain't giving it to them. How are you going to turn your head in the situation where this kid is asleep because he ain't got no energy, because he's hungry? You not going to feed a hungry kid? I mean, that would piss anybody off. **Officer Abdon:** Exactly. **Mike Africa Jr.:** So you know, this is what happens. *[[21:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1300s)]* **Officer Abdon:** And that's exactly why we like to relate everything back to the scriptures, because a lot of things that happen in the Bible was just taken away from us, so we didn't know what was the cause of a lot of things we read about. Like, everyone knows about the story of Moses. But the reason why Moses became Moses is because he saw the oppression of his people. That made him mad. He saw the Egyptians beating down his brothers. I want to read something for you. I want to see your thoughts on this. This is Ecclesiastes chapter 7 and verse 7. It says: **[Ecclesiastes 7:7](/bible/ecclesiastes/7#v7)** *[[22:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1338s)]* > [7](/bible/ecclesiastes/7#v7) Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart. - **Officer Abdon:** So Solomon, in all his wisdom, say, yo, oppression will make a wise man mad. - **Mike Africa Jr.:** Oh yeah. - **Officer Abdon:** So just like he was talking about, it's not that everybody just wakes up angry and they just want to fight and rebel. Because black people as a whole, we're a peaceful people, for the most part. - **Mike Africa Jr.:** We take a lot of punishment. - **Officer Abdon:** Exactly. Before we strike out. Exactly. But there's certain wise men in every generation that see the oppression, and it turns them into another man. - **Mike Africa Jr.:** Absolutely. That's exactly what happens in every single movement, and with the MOVE movement. Absolutely. And John Africa said, you know what, somebody got to do something. And it ain't even a thing of like you're replacing some other person or group that's doing something. No, we got to do something too. They're doing what they're doing; we got to do something too. We can't just let it be on them. We got to help them. *[[23:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1404s)]* **Officer Abdon:** So what happened with the MOVE 9 situation, with the police and the shooting? And I know it goes into a lot of your origin story, as far as what happened with your family. **Mike Africa Jr.:** Right. The resistance of MOVE to animal cruelty and elderly abuse and police brutality led to all of these different confrontations. MOVE would be at the Philadelphia Zoo protesting, and the cops come. MOVE don't want to see no cops. We protesting, we got the right to protest, there's no law we breaking. Cops come, MOVE don't want to see them. They get into it with each other: arguments, fights. I remember hearing about one incident where the police loaded up all of the men into the paddy wagons first, and then when the men were locked up in the paddy wagons, then they started beating on the women. So MOVE members heard things like that, and now when the police come, they want to fight. Because you just beat my wife. You just beat my sister. You just beat my daughter. So next time, I don't care if it wasn't Officer Abdon that hit my... You wore a uniform. Anybody in uniform come out here telling us to do anything, we gonna fight. And I am more than trained to fight you with my fists. You know what I'm saying? I ain't scared of nobody. I'll fight you with my fists. You got a club? So what, I got one too. You got a gun? You think they only sell guns to cops? So it was on that type of vibe. *[[25:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1540s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** So eventually it led to August 8th, 1978. The police came to MOVE's house. My mom was eight months pregnant with me at the time, and holding her two-year-old baby. My dad was right there with her, and other MOVE members, in the basement of the house. Police came. Fire department came, shooting water cannons. I say this sometimes: when we seeing the police shootings and stuff like that, I think people know the danger, the power of a bullet fired from a gun. But people don't really focus on the power of a water cannon, when them firefighters shoot that water out of them water cannons. **Officer Abdon:** Yeah. We see a little bit of the glimpse of it in the 60s with the civil rights. **Mike Africa Jr.:** See, in the 60s, those things were banned. You cannot use those against people. You're not supposed to use those on people; they're for putting out fires. The fire department is the police department with fire hoses instead of guns. **Officer Abdon:** That's funny you said that. There was a clip that went out with a brother. He came into a restaurant and he heard an old firefighter, it was a white man, basically confessing what happened when he was a firefighter. And it goes with the bombing, which we'll get into. He said he would go into buildings, and if he saw black children in those fires, he would leave them and let them die. And he confessed that. So like he's saying, firefighters are police, with fire hoses instead of guns. *[[27:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1647s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** The fire department, they were shooting those water cannons inside the house. Kids inside the house. My mom was pregnant; there was other pregnant women too, not just her. There was other women that had their two-year-old babies, not just her. The fire department had three of those hoses trained on the house. Then they dragged one inside the house. They took a chainsaw, cut a hole in the floor, so that they could fire it at the people directly. **Officer Abdon:** Wow. **Mike Africa Jr.:** Let me tell you something about how powerful those fire hoses are. They can shoot ten stories straight up into the air. Ten stories. If you get hit with one of them little powerful Super Soakers, them guns, they put your eye out. You hit somebody in your face, everybody know about that, that hurts. Ten stories straight up in the air. They can destabilize building structures. Firefighters are trained to do the exact opposite of what they did on August 8th. They're trained to never use them on buildings that they know people are inside of, because the building can collapse. So their intent that day was to kill or harm the MOVE members. They were tearing that building down with the people inside of it. *[[28:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1731s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** And then after the fire hoses couldn't force them out, they shot tear gas. Tear gas is very hot. I don't know if you've ever been hit with it before. **Officer Abdon:** No. **Mike Africa Jr.:** But it's hot. It burns. And it doesn't just have to get in your eyes. They call it tear gas like it only affects your eyes, but if you have on a mask that completely covers your eyes, you will still be affected by it. It'll still harm you. You can feel it inside of your ears. You can feel it as you breathe; it goes up into your head. You taste it; it burns your tongue. It gets on your skin. Take a hot pepper, like a habanero pepper, and rub it on your skin and feel. That's how it feels. It burns. Even when you take your clothes off, it sticks to your skin. If you have a shirt on when it happens and you take your shirt off, you can still feel it on your skin, burning. So that was thrown with the mothers, pregnant women, children. It was so much smoke from the tear gas and the smoke that it poured out of the house and started rushing out into the street. Looked like a fog machine on Halloween. And that's what actually caused MOVE members to exit the building, because they couldn't take the smoke. They couldn't take that tear gas. But before they exited the building, somebody fired a gun. *[[30:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1830s)]* **Officer Abdon:** Now I've heard about that. When the gun was fired, then everybody... So y'all exit the building, a gunshot was heard, then everyone fired? **Mike Africa Jr.:** No, no, no. A gunshot was heard. Everybody was shooting while the tear gas was happening. MOVE members were forced out of the house not by the gunshots and not by the water, but by the smoke. They couldn't breathe, and they couldn't see, so they had to feel their way out. And then once they came out, they were then arrested by the police. **Officer Abdon:** So what happened with the case, as far as the police officer? Was it James Ramp? **Mike Africa Jr.:** Right. So during the shooting, a police officer was shot and killed. His name was James Ramp. And of course police blamed it on MOVE. Every single one of them. Actually, none of them were specifically said... *[[31:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXts_fs8PR8&t=1905s)]* **Mike Africa Jr.:** This is the most bizarre case in Philadelphia history, Pennsylvania history, possibly American history. Twelve people were arrested. Two of them were found to not be MOVE members, so they were dismissed. Is this person a MOVE member? No, she was just happening to be in the house that day, because she is the girlfriend of one of the men. Oh, okay, well, dismiss her. Why is she here? What about this one? She's the wife. She's not the girlfriend, she's the wife of one of the MOVE members, and they have four children together. Is she a MOVE member? Well, we don't really know. Let's figure that out. It took nine months for them to figure it out. She's not a MOVE member. Let her go. Not: did she have a gun? Not: did anybody see her strike an officer? Did anyone see her commit any crime?
